title: Bananas (per lb)

drivers.name: price increase (1.5%)
drivers.evidence: Historical price elasticity suggests ~2.5-4% demand drop per 1% price rise; 1.5% increase implies ~3.5% lift reduction. Noise-adjusted estimate from recent $0.68 weeks: 0.95x vs baseline.

drivers.name: competitor store opening across the street
drivers.evidence: No prior data on similar events. Plausible downside due to foot traffic diversion. Low confidence; noise-adjusted estimate shrunk to -2.0%.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 438.2. A 1.5% price increase to $0.68 is modest but may suppress demand. The competitor opening across the street is a new, untested driver. No past data shows impact from a similar event. Price increase alone may reduce sales by ~3-5% based on elasticity, but evidence is thin. Competitor entry adds downside risk, but no historical lift or decline from similar events. Combined, the net effect is a small downward adjustment. The baseline already reflects seasonal and trend noise. No promotion or event justifies upward movement. Shrink toward 1.0 due to low evidence.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 438.2 | 5%-95%: 312.6 - 556.1 | 10%-90%: 346.5 - 529.1

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-21% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
